prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a plaintiff need not plead a prima facie case of discrimination to survive a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, but must allege facts supporting a plausible inference of discrimination.

Cite at least six decisions of the Fourth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. A plaintiff need not plead a prima facie case of discrimination. She must allege facts that make discrimination plausible.**

**A. The prima facie case is an evidentiary framework, not a pleading requirement.**

The *McDonnell Douglas* prima facie case is "an evidentiary standard, not a pleading requirement." *Swierkiewicz v. Sorema N.A.*, 534 U.S. 506, 510 (2002). The Supreme Court held that a plaintiff need not plead facts establishing each element of that framework to survive a motion to dismiss. *Id.* at 510–12. The framework is a flexible tool for sorting proof at summary judgment or trial. It does not set the minimum a complaint must contain, and it can vary with the facts of a given case. *Id.* at 511–12. Rule 8(a)(2) requires only "a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief."

The Fourth Circuit applies this rule. A Title VII plaintiff "is not required to plead facts that constitute a prima facie case in order to survive a motion to dismiss." *Coleman v. Md. Court of Appeals*, 626 F.3d 187, 190 (4th Cir. 2010) (citing *Swierkiewicz*, 534 U.S. at 510–15); *accord Woods v. City of Greensboro*, 855 F.3d 639, 648 (4th Cir. 2017); *McCleary-Evans v. Md. Dep't of Transp.*, 780 F.3d 582, 584–85 (4th Cir. 2015). A court that dismisses a complaint because it omits an element of the prima facie case applies the wrong standard. *See Coleman*, 626 F.3d at 190–91; *Woods*, 855 F.3d at 648.

**B. *Twombly* and *Iqbal* did not revive a prima facie pleading requirement, but they do require plausibility.**

*Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly*, 550 U.S. 544 (2007), and *Ashcroft v. Iqbal*, 556 U.S. 662 (2009), did not displace *Swierkiewicz*. They did add that a complaint must contain enough factual matter, accepted as true, to "state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face." *Twombly*, 550 U.S. at 570; *Iqbal*, 556 U.S. at 678. The Fourth Circuit has reconciled the two lines of authority. The prima facie elements are not the pleading test. But a plaintiff must still allege facts that, taken as true, support a reasonable inference that the employer took the adverse action because of a protected characteristic. *Coleman*, 626 F.3d at 190–91; *McCleary-Evans*, 780 F.3d at 585; *Woods*, 855 F.3d at 648. Elements of the prima facie case may help a court judge plausibility. They are not a checklist the complaint must satisfy.

On a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, the court accepts well-pleaded facts as true and draws reasonable inferences in the plaintiff's favor. It need not credit bare legal conclusions. *Francis v. Giacomelli*, 588 F.3d 186, 192–93 (4th Cir. 2009). Plausibility "is not a probability requirement." *Iqbal*, 556 U.S. at 678. A complaint survives even if the court doubts that the plaintiff will ultimately prevail, and even if an innocent explanation also fits the facts. *See Woods*, 855 F.3d at 648–49; *Francis*, 588 F.3d at 193.

**C. The Complaint alleges facts supporting a plausible inference of discrimination.**

*McCleary-Evans* shows what separates a sufficient complaint from an insufficient one. There, the plaintiff alleged only that decisionmakers must have been biased, and the court held that such speculation did not make her claim plausible. 780 F.3d at 585–86. Plaintiff's Complaint is different. It does not rest on the bare assertion that the employer discriminated. It pleads specific facts: [identify protected class; qualifications and satisfactory performance; the adverse action and its timing; the identity and treatment of comparators outside the protected class; and any statements, departures from policy, or shifting explanations]. Taken as true, these facts permit a reasonable inference that [protected characteristic] was the reason for the adverse action. Nothing more is required at this stage.

Defendant's motion argues that the Complaint fails to establish one or more elements of a prima facie case, such as [similarly situated comparator / satisfactory performance]. That argument demands more than Rule 8 requires. *Coleman*, 626 F.3d at 190; *Woods*, 855 F.3d at 648. Whether Plaintiff's comparators are similarly situated, and whether Defendant's stated reason is pretextual, are fact-intensive questions. Discovery will answer them, and they cannot be resolved on the pleadings. *See Swierkiewicz*, 534 U.S. at 512. The Fourth Circuit has reversed dismissals that held complaints to a prima facie standard when the pleaded facts supported a plausible inference of discrimination. *See Woods*, 855 F.3d at 648–52; *Coleman*, 626 F.3d at 190–91.

The Complaint states a plausible claim. The Court should deny the motion to dismiss.
